items.title: Computing on Bits: Circuits and Processors

slides.title: Our Journey So Far…
rows: Binary digits + context: numbers, text, pixels and colors, instructions
School mathematics (logic, set theory); logic operations (NOT, NOR, …, NAND)
Logic gates from electronic components (today: transistors)
Adder circuits and circuits for other arithmetic functions: a general-purpose calculator!
Function selector, arithmetic/logic unit, control unit, registers: voilà, a CPU!
Instruction sets, machine code and assembly language

slides.title: Why do we look at Assembly Code?
points: Assembly code makes normally hidden processor state visible: it lets us look into the very essence of computing
slides.lead: Examples you will see today and just after the break:
defs: the memory address of the next instruction (like 0x100 to 0x108 in [our small ISA](https://hyperdecks.github.io/computersystems/03-processors/html/#/33))
16 named locations for 64-bit values (addresses and data); some special-purpose, others general-purpose
status of the most recent arithmetic or logical instruction (needed for if/else and loops!)

slides.title: Assembly Overview
points: From a given starting position, there is a unique encoding of bytes to machine instructions
More common instructions have shorter encodings
There are different ISAs for different architectures (lecture: x86-64; exercise: ARMv8)
There are different styles within one architecture (AT&T vs. Intel)

points.text: Compiler optimizations have a large impact on the program!
sub: Replace slow (machine) operations with faster ones

aside.code:
Intel syntax
mov   eax,[ebx+20h]
add   eax,[ebx+ecx*2h]
lea   eax,[ebx+ecx]

AT&T syntax
movl  0x20(%ebx),%eax
addl  (%ebx,%ecx,0x2),%eax
leal  (%ebx,%ecx),%eax

slides.title: x86-64 Registers
points: x86-64 has 16 named registers
These can store 64 bits each
They are very close to the processor: it can access register values almost instantaneously (i.e., within one processor cycle, multiple billion times per second)
Very informative: [Wikibooks: x86 Architecture](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/X86_Assembly/X86_Architecture)

aside.alt: Table of the 16 x86-64 integer registers and their usage: %rax return value, %rdi to %r9 arguments 1 to 6, %rsp stack pointer, others caller or callee saved
aside.caption: Source: Lora Charles, [slideplayer.com](http://slideplayer.com/slide/9679824/)

slides.title: x86-64 Registers: Names for Parts of a Register
points: %rdi, %rax, %rbx, %rcx, etc. denote the entire 64 bits (i.e., the so-called quad-word) of a register
To address the other, low-order portions, other names are used:

aside.alt: Table with the 64-bit register names and the names of their lower 32, 16 and 8 bits, from rax, eax, ax, al to r15, r15d, r15w, r15b

slides.title: x86-64 Registers: Who Saves What?

callout.text: «Function calls are just an elaborate illusion»

defs: the caller of a procedure needs to take care of these registers, no guarantees: foo() may override %r10
the caller can trust that these hold the same value after a call: main can trust that %rbx is unchanged. If foo() uses that register, it needs to restore the value before returning to main()
indicates the current position in the run-time stack (more on this next week)

slides.title: Assembly Operands
slides.lead: An x86-64 instruction has zero to three operands (`ret`, `notq %rax`, `addq %rdi, %rax`, `imulq $300, %rdi, %rax`). Operands are always one of three types:

slides.title: What's the value and type of each of these operands?
points: `%rax`
`(%rax,%rdx,4)`

aside.code:
Given register contents
%rax   0x100
%rcx   0x1
%rdx   0x3

Given memory contents
0x100  0xFF
0x104  0xAB
0x108  0x13
0x10C  0x11

slides.after: Memory is byte-addressable; the table simply shows one 4-byte word per row.

slides.title: Value and Type of Each Operand
Why exactly 0x11?
points: %rax contains 0x100 (a memory address, i.e., a pointer)
The parentheses ( ) tell us that we need to dereference 0x10C: Mem[0x10C] = 0x11

slides.title: Data Movement
slides.lead: Data movement from source to destination.

groups.heading: x86-64 data movement instructions (excerpt)
points: `mov(b/w/l/q)`: move byte/word/double-word/quad-word
`movabsq`: move an absolute 64-bit immediate value

groups.heading: Observations
points: We can move chunks of 8, 16, 32, and 64 bits
Movement from memory to memory is not permitted in general!

slides.title: Moving Immediate Values

slides.title: Moving between Registers and Memory
slides.lead: Remember: d(Rb,Ri,s) = Mem[d + Rb + Ri × s]

slides.title: Binky's Data Movement Exercise
points: Compiled with the compiler explorer (optimization level `-O1`)
Observation: C pointers are simply addresses in memory
Arguments are assigned to registers in order: %rdi → %rsi → %rdx → %rcx → %r8 → %r9
In this example, `xpointer` goes into %rdi, `y` goes into %rsi

slides.title: Sample Exam Question (6pt ~ 6min)
slides.lead: (6pt) Complete the figure given the following information:
points: Register RSI contains the value 12
Register RDX contains the value 0xFFFFFFFF
Register RAX represents a pointer to memory location 0xFFFF0000
What is the result of the processor executing the instruction `movq (%rax), %rsi`?
The memory location immediately below 0xFFFF0000 is called 0xFFFF0008. Why?

slides.title: Sample Exam Question: Solution
points: `movq (%rax), %rsi` reads the quad-word at the address in %rax (0xFFFF0000) into %rsi: 12 becomes 68
A quad-word has 8 bytes, and memory is byte-addressable: the next quad-word starts at 0xFFFF0008

slides.title: Arithmetic and Logic Operations
rows: increments the value stored at the memory location pointed to by %rsp by $1
reduces the value in %rdx by the value in %rax
binary OR, denoted using the pipe symbol: 001b | 100b = ???b
shifts the value in %rax left by 3 bits: multiplies it by 8
`leaq S, D`: works like mov, but only computes the address and does not access memory at all

slides.title: Arithmetic and Logic Operations Exercise: Without imulq
slides.code:
arith:
  orq    %rsi, %rdi
  subq   %rsi, %rdi
  movq   %rdi, %rax
  addq   %rax, %rax
  addq   %rdi, %rax
  salq   $4, %rax
points: %rax = t1, then t1 + t1 = 2 × t1, then + t1 = 3 × t1
Shifting left by 4 bits multiplies by 16: 3 × 16 = 48
[Lecture 1: Shifting](https://hyperdecks.github.io/computersystems/01-information/html/#/72)

slides.title: Potential Exam Question (5p)
slides.lead: `xorq %rcx, %rcx` computes a bit-by-bit xor of a register's contents with the same register's contents, and stores the result in that register.
items: What would be any alternative instruction to achieve the same result?
Can you speculate why the compiler typically chooses to use the xor option over this?
slides.notes: Alternative: movq $0, %rcx. The encoding of xorq %rcx, %rcx might be shorter than for the movq $0, %rcx operation.

slides.title: Conditionals Intuition: The Assembly

callout.text: How exactly do cmpq and jle work?

slides.code:
conditionalsExample(long):
        pushq   %rbp
        movq    %rsp, %rbp
        movq    %rdi, -8(%rbp)
        cmpq    $0, -8(%rbp)
        jle     .L6
        movl    $1, %eax
        jmp     .L4
.L6:
        nop
        movl    $0, %eax
.L4:
        popq    %rbp
        ret
points: Same for both C versions!
Variable x is located in %rdi

slides.title: Condition Code Registers
points: Single-bit registers («flags») that hold attributes of the most recent arithmetic, logical or comparison operation
Logical operations always set CF and OF to zero (there cannot be an overflow)
Shift operations set CF to the last bit shifted out; OF is defined only for 1-bit shifts
defs: carry flag: set on a carry out
zero flag: set if the result is zero
sign flag: set if the result is negative
overflow flag: set on a [2's complement overflow](https://hyperdecks.github.io/computersystems/01-information/html/#/68)

slides.title: Condition Codes
slides.lead: We do not have to execute arithmetic or logic operations just to set condition codes. We can set them explicitly through cmp and test:
points: `cmp` does a `sub`, but without remembering the result. It just remembers the condition codes
`test` does an `and`, but without remembering the result. It just remembers the condition codes

aside.code:
cmp(b/w/l/q) A, B    # CCs from B - A
test(b/w/l/q) A, B   # CCs from A & B

testq %rax, %rax
# compare %rax to itself to see
# whether its content is negative,
# zero or positive

slides.title: Control Flow: Conditionals
points: Logic, arithmetic and comparison instructions (testq and cmpq) set condition codes
Conditional jumps and conditional moves read them
These jumps and moves implement conditionals, switches and loops in a computer system

slides.title: Condition Codes to Conditionally Jump
rows: to the location read from memory
if not equal (zero flag not set)

slides.title: Condition Codes to Conditionally Jump: Signed and Unsigned
rows: if greater / if not less or equal (>)
if greater or equal / if not less (>=)

slides.title: Conditional Jumps Example
slides.code:
checkEquals(long, long):
	pushq   %rbp
	movq    %rsp, %rbp
	movq    %rdi, -8(%rbp)
	movq    %rsi, -16(%rbp)
	movq    -8(%rbp), %rax
	cmpq    -16(%rbp), %rax
	jne     .L2
	movl    $1, %eax
	jmp     .L3
.L2:
	movl    $0, %eax
.L3:
	popq    %rbp
	ret
points: C: `long checkEquals(long x, long y) { if (x == y) return 1; else return 0; }`
Where do the arguments go? x → %rdi, y → %rsi

slides.title: Extensive Conditional Jumps Exercise

callout.text: Homework! Write the C code of inkognito

slides.lead: This is NOT an example of a good exam question, but it's good for training.
slides.code:
inkognito(long, long):
  pushq %rbp
  movq  %rsp, %rbp
  movq  $0, -8(%rbp)
.L3:
  cmpq  $0, %rdi
  jle   .L2
  movq  %rsi, %rax
  addq  %rax, -8(%rbp)
  subq  $1, %rdi
  jmp   .L3
.L2:
  movq  -8(%rbp), %rax
  popq  %rbp
  ret
points: `long inkognito(long x, long y) { … }`
Remember: arguments are assigned to registers in order: %rdi → %rsi → %rdx → %rcx → %r8 → %r9

slides.title: Extensive Conditional Jumps Exercise: Step by Step
slides.code:
inkognito(long, long):
  pushq %rbp
  movq  %rsp, %rbp
  movq  $0, -8(%rbp)    # store a $0 in memory
.L3:
  cmpq  $0, %rdi        # CCs from (%rdi - $0)
  jle   .L2             # jump if less or equal…
  movq  %rsi, %rax      # %rax = y
  addq  %rax, -8(%rbp)  # add %rax to the value in memory
  subq  $1, %rdi        # %rdi = %rdi - 1
  jmp   .L3             # jump!
.L2:
  movq  -8(%rbp), %rax  # move the value from memory to %rax
  popq  %rbp
  ret

slides.title: Extensive Conditional Jumps Exercise: Cleaned Up…
points: For x > 0, inkognito adds y to itself x times: it multiplies x and y
Remember: multiplying is just repeated adding ([lecture 1](https://hyperdecks.github.io/computersystems/01-information/html/#/19))

slides.title: Any Questions / Comments / Doubts / Concerns?
slides.heading: Take-Homes
points: You have seen many frequently occurring assembly instructions in the x86-64 ISA
Conditionals and loops are simply implemented as «jumps» on the machine. In C, we call these «gotos»; the ARMv8 ISA calls them «branches»
Get a feeling for assembly by training, and by experimenting with the compiler explorer at [godbolt.org](https://godbolt.org/)
Exercise 2 gives you an opportunity to train: among other tasks, you will reverse-engineer a program from assembly
